name: Place de la Bastille
short_description: Historic square where the infamous fortress-prison once stood, stormed on July 14, 1789

beats.script_body: The Bastille was far from the grim dungeon of popular imagination. It functioned as a luxury prison for well-connected inmates. Voltaire completed his tragedy Oedipe here, composing verses and dining well. The Marquis de Sade draped his cell walls with fabric and had his own furniture brought in. When the fortress was finally stormed on July 14, 1789, the liberators found only seven prisoners inside — a far cry from the hundreds the revolutionaries imagined they would free.
physical_cues: Look for the outline of the fortress traced in paving stones on the ground
beats.source_passage: Voltaire completed his tragedy Oedipe here; the Marquis de Sade draped his cell walls
beats.fact_check_notes: Voltaire's release date corrected from 1717 to 1718.

beats.script_body: The Marquis de Sade was transferred to the Bastille from Vincennes in 1784. He fashioned a megaphone from a funnel and shouted to passersby that prisoners were being murdered inside. The authorities removed him in early July 1789 — just days before the storming. At the Bastille he wrote some of his most notorious works, including Justine.
beats.source_passage: Sade fashioned a megaphone and shouted to passersby; transferred from Vincennes 1784
beats.fact_check_notes: Sade's works corrected — Justine was written at the Bastille, not Vincennes.

beats.script_body: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 became the founding myth of the French Revolution, yet the reality was far less dramatic. Finance minister Necker had already drawn up plans to demolish the fortress. When the mob broke in, they found only seven bewildered prisoners — four forgers, two madmen, and a young nobleman imprisoned at his family's request.
beats.source_passage: Necker had planned demolition; only 7 prisoners found

name: Temple du Marais
short_description: Mansart's 17th-century domed church, originally built for the Visitandine order, now a Protestant temple since Napoleon's decree of 1803.

beats.script_body: This small church boasts one of Paris's most influential domes. Francois Mansart designed it with a circular plan and a striking 35-metre dome that became the model for two of France's greatest buildings: the Val-de-Grace and the Invalides. Napoleon gave the church to the Protestants in 1803, and it has served as a Reformed temple ever since.
physical_cues: Notice the circular plan of the interior
beats.source_passage: Mansart's 35m dome became the model for Val-de-Grace and Invalides; Napoleon gave to Protestants 1803

beats.script_body: The Visitandine convent was a fashionable retreat for society women tired of worldly life. Madame de La Fayette, author of La Princesse de Cleves, retired here as Soeur Angelique. But not all residents took to piety: the tempestuous Hortense Mancini, niece of Cardinal Mazarin, once poured black ink into the holy water font.
beats.source_passage: Visitandines society retreat; Madame de La Fayette as Soeur Angelique; Hortense Mancini black ink in holy water

name: Hotel de Mayenne
short_description: 16th-century Marais mansion associated with Henri III's favourites and the Catholic League's assassination plots.

beats.script_body: In 1578, a savage duel took place near this mansion. Quelus, one of Henri III's favourites, was stabbed eighteen times. The distraught King ordered straw laid on the street to muffle passing carriages so his dying companion could rest in peace. The Hotel de Mayenne later became a centre for the Catholic League, and within these walls the assassination of Henri III was plotted.
beats.source_passage: 1578 duel, Quelus stabbed 18 times, Henri III ordered straw on street

name: Place des Vosges
short_description: Paris's oldest planned square, surrounded by harmonious brick-and-stone mansions

beats.script_body: Henri IV dreamed of making Paris a centre of silk manufacture, hoping to rival Lyon and undercut costly Italian imports. He brought 200 Italian workers to the site of this square and planted mulberry trees for their silkworms. But the northern climate defeated the enterprise — the silkworms simply could not survive Parisian winters, and the project was abandoned.
beats.source_passage: Henri IV brought 200 Italian workers; silkworms couldn't survive winters

beats.script_body: The Pavillon du Roi dominates the south side of the square, grander than the other 36 houses that form the harmonious ensemble. The square was inaugurated in 1612 with a spectacular three-day celebration for the double wedding of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, and his sister Elisabeth with the future Philip IV of Spain. It was renamed Place des Vosges in 1800, honouring the first department to pay its taxes to the new Republic.
physical_cues: Notice the Pavillon du Roi on the south side, taller than the rest
beats.source_passage: Pavillon du Roi, 36 houses, inaugurated 1612, renamed Place des Vosges 1800

beats.script_body: On September 8, 1656, Christina of Sweden made a spectacular entry into the square. The former queen, who had abdicated her throne two years earlier, arrived in Paris amid great fanfare and was received with elaborate ceremony at Place Royale.
beats.source_passage: Christina of Sweden's spectacular entry September 8 1656

name: Musee Victor Hugo
short_description: Victor Hugo's former apartment at 6 Place des Vosges, now a museum dedicated to the great writer's life and works.

beats.script_body: Victor Hugo moved to this apartment at 6 Place des Vosges in 1832 and lived here for sixteen years. In these rooms he wrote the drama Ruy Blas and sketched out the early plans for his masterwork Les Miserables. The apartment preserves his furniture and many of his own drawings and decorative pieces.
physical_cues: Look for number 6 on the southeast corner of Place des Vosges
Hugo's apartment on the second floor
beats.source_passage: Hugo moved here 1832, wrote Ruy Blas, sketched Les Miserables

beats.script_body: Hugo's domestic life at Place des Vosges was turbulent. His wife Adele carried on an affair with their close friend, the critic Sainte-Beuve. Hugo himself began a passionate liaison with the actress Juliette Drouet, who lived nearby. A secret back staircase allowed discreet comings and goings — the arrangement lasted for fifty years until Drouet's death.
beats.source_passage: Adele's affair with Sainte-Beuve; Hugo's liaison with Juliette Drouet; secret back staircase

name: Hotel de Sully
short_description: Magnificent 17th-century mansion with a storied past, from its gambler builder to Voltaire's beating.

beats.script_body: The Hotel de Sully was built in 1624 for Mesme Gallet, a notorious gambler who squandered his fortune on a single night's losses and had to sell up. The aged Duc de Sully bought it next, but his young wife's infidelities were legendary. The pragmatic duke installed a separate staircase so her lovers could come and go without crossing his path.
physical_cues: Look for the ornate Renaissance facade
beats.source_passage: Built 1624 for gambler Gallet; aged Duc de Sully installed separate staircase for wife's lovers

beats.script_body: In the early 18th century, Voltaire was beaten up by the lackeys of the Prince de Rohan near the Hotel de Sully. The young writer challenged the prince to a duel, but Rohan's aristocratic family had Voltaire thrown into the Bastille instead. Upon his release, Voltaire left for England — an exile that would profoundly shape his political philosophy and produce his influential Letters on the English.
physical_cues: Hotel de Sully entrance on rue Saint-Antoine
beats.source_passage: Voltaire beaten up by Prince de Rohan, challenged to duel, imprisoned, went to England

name: Hotel de Sens
short_description: One of the oldest civilian buildings in Paris, a medieval fortress-mansion with a scandalous royal history.

beats.script_body: The Hotel de Sens is one of the oldest civilian monuments in Paris. Its most dramatic episode came in 1606, when the ageing Queen Margot — Henri IV's first wife — was living here. As her coach was leaving, the Comte de Vermond shot dead a rival lover on the very threshold. Margot, enraged, had Vermond arrested, and he was beheaded the following day in front of the hotel.
physical_cues: Look at the medieval turrets and Gothic entrance
Imagine the threshold where the shooting took place
beats.source_passage: Queen Margot, Comte de Vermond killed rival on threshold 1606, beheaded next day

name: Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis
short_description: Baroque Jesuit church on rue Saint-Antoine, noted for its musical heritage and Counter-Reformation architecture.

beats.script_body: The church of Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis was the stage for some of the greatest preaching and music of the 17th century. Marc-Antoine Charpentier composed his celebrated Miserere for these acoustics. The Jesuit preacher Bourdaloue was so popular that ladies would arrive six hours early to secure a seat — they even had a special hat named after him, designed to be worn during his lengthy sermons.
physical_cues: Listen to the acoustics of the baroque interior
beats.source_passage: Charpentier's Miserere; Bourdaloue preaching; hat named after him

beats.script_body: The Jesuits arrived in Paris in 1580 and established themselves on rue Saint-Antoine. Louis XIII laid the cornerstone of this church in 1627, and Cardinal Richelieu celebrated its first mass in 1641. The imposing baroque facade, unusual for Paris, reflects the Counter-Reformation confidence of the Jesuit order.
beats.source_passage: Jesuits arrived 1580, Louis XIII laid cornerstone 1627, Richelieu celebrated mass 1641

name: Village Saint-Paul
short_description: A cluster of antique courtyards and shops in the former grounds of a medieval church destroyed by Norse invaders.

beats.script_body: The Village Saint-Paul is a warren of interconnected courtyards filled with antique dealers and curiosity shops. It takes its name from a 7th-century church that once stood here — one of the oldest in Paris — which was destroyed by the Norsemen during their devastating raids on the city.
beats.source_passage: Named after 7th-century church destroyed by Norsemen

name: Hotel Lamoignon
short_description: Renaissance mansion housing the Historical Library of Paris, built for Henri II's illegitimate daughter.

beats.script_body: The Hotel Lamoignon was built for Diane de France, the illegitimate daughter of Henri II and a Piedmontese woman. Later, President Lamoignon established a literary academy here that attracted Racine, Boileau, and Madame de Sevigne. It was also the site of the trial of the notorious poisoner La Brinvilliers, whose crimes horrified 17th-century Paris.
physical_cues: Look for the hunting motifs on the facade — a nod to Diane, the huntress
beats.source_passage: Built for Diane de France; Lamoignon's literary academy; trial of La Brinvilliers

name: Synagogue de la rue Pavee
short_description: Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau synagogue, the only religious building by the famed Metro architect.

beats.script_body: This is the only religious building ever designed by Hector Guimard, the Art Nouveau architect famous for his Paris Metro entrances. Its undulating facade in concrete is unmistakably Guimard. He married an American heiress, Miss Oppenheimer, suggesting a personal connection to the Jewish community that may have inspired this commission.
physical_cues: Look at the sinuous Art Nouveau facade
Compare Guimard's style to the Metro entrances you may have seen
beats.source_passage: Hector Guimard Art Nouveau, only religious building he created, married Miss Oppenheimer

name: Rue des Rosiers
short_description: The historic heart of the Marais Jewish quarter, known as the Pletzl, with deep roots in Paris's Jewish heritage.

beats.script_body: Rue des Rosiers is the backbone of the pletzel — Yiddish for 'little square' — the historic Jewish quarter of the Marais. At number 20 stood the Hotel des Juifs, a reminder of the community's deep roots here. The street's most heartbreaking memorial marks the deportation of 165 pupils from a local school during the Occupation — children who never returned.
physical_cues: Walk along rue des Rosiers and notice the Hebrew shop signs
Look for the Hotel des Juifs plaque at number 20
beats.source_passage: Backbone of pletzel; Hotel des Juifs at no 20; 165 pupils deported from school

beats.script_body: On the wall of the school on rue des Rosiers, an inscription reads 'N'OUBLIEZ PAS' — Do Not Forget. It commemorates the 165 Jewish pupils who were deported from this school during the Occupation and murdered in the death camps. None survived.
physical_cues: Look for the N'OUBLIEZ PAS inscription on the school wall
beats.source_passage: N'OUBLIEZ PAS inscription; 165 deported pupils

name: Hotel Amelot de Bisseuil
short_description: Magnificent Marais mansion where Beaumarchais wrote The Marriage of Figaro and arranged arms for the American Revolution.

beats.script_body: Beaumarchais lived in this magnificent mansion from 1776 and wrote Le Mariage de Figaro here — the play that scandalised the aristocracy and foreshadowed the Revolution. But he was also a secret agent: from this very address he set up a front company to supply arms and ammunition to the American revolutionaries fighting for independence from Britain, with the tacit approval of Louis XVI.
physical_cues: Look at the ornate portal with its sculpted cherubs
beats.source_passage: Beaumarchais from 1776 wrote Le Mariage de Figaro; set up arms company for American Revolution

name: Notre-Dame-des-Blancs-Manteaux
short_description: Church named after medieval white-robed begging friars from Marseilles, later replaced by black-gowned Guillemites.

beats.script_body: The church takes its name from the white-robed begging friars who arrived from Marseilles in 1258, seeking alms in the neighbourhood. When Saint Louis suppressed mendicant orders, they were replaced by the black-gowned Guillemites — yet the name 'Blancs-Manteaux' (white cloaks) stuck, a ghostly reminder of those original penitents. Sartre later commemorated the street in a poem.
beats.source_passage: White-robed beggars from Marseilles 1258; replaced by black-gowned Guillemites; Sartre poem

name: La Force Prison Site
short_description: Former prison where the Princesse de Lamballe was murdered during the September Massacres of 1792.

beats.script_body: On this site stood La Force prison, the scene of one of the Revolution's most horrifying episodes. In September 1792, during the massacres, the Princesse de Lamballe — Marie-Antoinette's closest friend — was dragged from her cell and murdered by the mob. Her head was impaled on a pike and paraded to the Temple prison, where it was thrust before the windows of the captive Queen.
physical_cues: The prison has been demolished — only the street layout preserves its memory
beats.source_passage: Princesse de Lamballe murdered September 1792; head impaled and displayed before Marie-Antoinette
